tagline: Quaker settlement, a cotton gin namesake and a railway town
intro: Football Road belongs to North Carolina’s Piedmont collection of scenic byways. The North Carolina Department of Transportation describes its byways as alternatives to major highways, chosen to introduce the state’s history, geography and culture.

Snow Camp’s history reaches back to Quakers who migrated from Pennsylvania to the Cane Creek valley in the mid-1700s. Carrboro developed beside the State University Railroad spur, with settlement increasing after Thomas F. Lloyd built a gristmill near the depot in 1898.
From Snow Camp, Eli Whitney lies to the east, where Greensboro-Chapel Hill Road meets NC 87. Carrboro lies directly west of Chapel Hill, home of the University of North Carolina’s flagship campus.

moments.title: Snow Camp
moments.text: Snow Camp’s Quaker history has a physical center at the spring, where several buildings from the early settlement remain. Friends from Pennsylvania came to the Cane Creek valley in the mid-1700s and established Spring Meeting. The congregation remains active; its present meeting house is the fourth, built in 1907. That wooden building has pointed Gothic Revival windows and a small cupola. Another part of the community’s history centers on Simon Dixon’s gristmill: Cornwallis seized his home and mill for temporary quarters after the Battle of Guilford Courthouse in 1781. Dixon’s gristmill continued operating into the 20th century.

moments.title: Eli Whitney
moments.text: A cotton gin gave Eli Whitney its name, though the inventor’s life had no direct connection to the community. The crossroads sits at NC 87 and Greensboro-Chapel Hill Road, east of Snow Camp. The community’s former school has its own history of change. Eli Whitney High was built in the 1920s, served the community until 1974 and was demolished the next year. The former gymnasium has a different role now: it is the Eli Whitney Community Center.

moments.title: Carrboro
moments.text: Carrboro began as West End, a settlement beside the terminus of the State University Railroad spur in 1882. State law kept the railway at least a mile from the university campus to protect student morals and study habits. Thomas F. Lloyd built a steam-powered gristmill near the depot in 1898; it became the Alberta Cotton Mill. Mill No. 4, the original Alberta mill, closed in 1930; passenger trains stopped serving the town in 1936. When demolition threatened the abandoned mill in 1975, a community petition and fundraising effort secured its restoration as Carr Mill Mall.
